title.en: The Cooking-Pot That Turned Ashes to Gold

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: hearthside compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊灶邊院落）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXIX

summary.en: A man makes his wife cook nightly in a battered old pot that turns the fire's ashes to gold; he gathers the golden ashes secretly each night. A young man who has spied on him trades a fine new pot for the old one — and is said to have spent his life cooking thereafter, earning the nickname Chop, or Food.
summary.zh: 丈夫命妻子夜夜用一口破舊炊鍋煮飯——此鍋能將灶灰化為黃金，他每夜趁人睡熟偷偷收取金灰。村中青年窺得蹊蹺，趁丈夫外出以新鍋換走舊鍋。相傳此人自此終生煮飯，得了「喬普」（食物）的綽號。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; magic-object tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: A man once brought home to his wife a very old cooking-pot and told her to use it every day when preparing the evening meal. The woman was not pleased at the idea of using such a battered vessel and feared her friends would ridicule her, but she dared not disobey and began to use the pot as he demanded. Little did she guess that the pot was a magic one, with the virtue of turning the ashes of the fire, on which it rested, into gold. Every night the husband crept out, when all were asleep in the huts around the compound, and gathered together these golden ashes, which he stored safely away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day a young man in the village came to the woman while her husband was absent and asked a favour of her: he had taken a fancy to her old cooking-pot and would give her a fine new one in exchange. The woman hesitated, but she was ashamed of the ugly old pot and was glad of an excuse to be rid of it. When her husband found what she had done he was very angry and beat her soundly; but it was too late to recover the pot, as the young man was already far away in the forest. Naturally he had not obtained the pot without knowing its secret, for he had observed the actions of the man who so mysteriously collected the ashes every night; and it is said that from that day the young man spent his life cooking, and so earned the name of Chop, or Food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXIX (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Parrot That Could Not Lie

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: threshold near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊門檻）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXX

summary.en: A grey parrot with the habit of correcting every untruth first exposes its lying owner, then its new one — and when the new owner is searched for stolen goods, the parrot's "He lies!" sends the searchers back until the buried hoard is found. In rage the thief wrings the bird's neck, but the truth is out.
summary.zh: 灰鸚鵡慣於當眾揭穿謊言，先拆穿原主人的虛言，再令新主人的謊話無所遁形。新主人竊得財物埋於深坑，搜查者無功將退之際，鸚鵡一聲「他撒謊！」引人重搜，終在小木樁標記的坑中起出贓物。盛怒的竊賊扭斷鳥頸，然而真相已大白。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; truth-telling animal tale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a grey parrot which knew how to speak and had the habit of correcting anybody who did not tell the truth. The parrot was the pet of an untruthful woman, who found the habit so inconvenient that she at length decided to get rid of it. One day a neighbour was passing her house, and the woman called out to him from the threshold to come and see the beautiful tame parrot which she intended to give him as a present. Asked why she desired to part with so beautiful a bird, she replied: "Because it eats a great deal, and I am poor." The parrot cried out: "She lies!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: The neighbour took the bird home, and when his wife asked where he had found it, he said it had flown down and perched on his shoulder as he came through the forest — but the parrot quickly cried: "He lies!" The man was dishonest and had stolen many articles which he buried in a deep hole unknown to anybody. When the thefts were discovered, the searchers found nothing in his house and were about to accept his denial, but the parrot cried: "He lies!" In rage he seized the bird and twisted its neck, but the suspicion of the searchers was aroused, and eventually they discovered the hole, which was marked with a little stake, and all the stolen articles were found. Had it not been for the truthful parrot, the secret would never have been revealed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXX (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Oyo-Ile (Old Oyo), Nigeria (symbolic pin: the hill chosen for the new capital)
region.zh: 奈及利亞舊奧約城（象徵定位：擬建新都的山丘）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXI

summary.en: King Abipa resolves to move his court to a new capital on a hill; four nobles send slaves — a hunchback, an albino, a leper, and a dwarf — to haunt the site crying "No room!" His hunters capture the "ghosts," and at a banquet each rebel noble is served his beer by his own supposed spectre. The court removes without opposition, and Abipa is known ever after as the Ghost-Catcher.
summary.zh: 阿比帕王決定遷都於一座悅目的山丘；四位不願遷移的貴族遂派出各自的奴隸——駝背、白化者、痲瘋者、侏儒——裝鬼在山上高呼「無地可容！」。王遣獵人將「鬼」盡數捉回，宴席上又命各「鬼」為其主子上酒。四位貴族見奉酒者正是自家奴隸，嚇得不敢作聲。朝廷順利遷都，阿比帕自此被稱為「捉鬼王」。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; the tale is attached to Abipa's historical refoundation of Oyo-Ile's capital. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: King Abipa took a fancy to remove his whole court to a new capital, and for this purpose decided to build a town on a certain hill which pleased him. His nobles did not at all desire the change, and some of them met together to make a plan which would turn the King away from his project: they agreed to send certain slaves of repulsive appearance to haunt the hill after the manner of ghosts. One noble sent a hunchback, another an albino, another a leper, and a fourth a dwarf. When the King's messengers arrived to survey the hill, they saw these strange apparitions leaping about with torches in their hands, shouting with one voice: "Ko si aye! Ko si aye!" (No room! No room!). They returned in terror and told him the hill was haunted by ghosts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: However, one of the royal advisers suspected a plot and advised the King to send hunters to the hill to capture the "ghosts." The hunters returned with the supposed ghosts, who were in abject terror at being discovered; instead of killing them, the King kept them hidden and invited all his nobles to a banquet. When they had feasted merrily, he sent round to each noble a calabash of beer by the hands of a slave: what was the dismay of the four rebellious nobles to receive the calabash, one from his hunchback, another from his albino, and the others from the hands of the leper and the dwarf! Obviously the plot had been discovered, and all four expected death; but the wise Abipa said no word about the matter, and the banquet ended in silence. Soon afterwards the court removed to the new town without any opposition, and henceforth the King was known as the Ghost-Catcher.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXI (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise Traps the Elephant and Wins the Princess

region.en: Yoruba royal town (symbolic pin: pit outside the town walls, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約城外陷坑）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXII

summary.en: An elephant ravages the country, escaping every trap by charms, and the King offers his daughter to whoever can destroy it. Tortoise flatters the beast that the people wish to crown him, leads him onto a velvet-draped platform over a pit, and the hunters slay him. Cheated of the promised bride, Tortoise turns the field-mice loose on the crops, then sells peace for the princess — and settles the mice with a promised feast before each harvest.
summary.zh: 大象肆虐田園，諸般陷阱因牠通曉符咒而無效；國王懸賞女兒為妻。龜君吹捧大象「舉國盼你登基」，引牠踏上蓋著天鵝絨與豹皮的高臺，臺下正是陷坑，獵手隨即誅之。國王卻嫌龜君卑小而悔婚，龜君便放縱田鼠毀莊稼；王被迫允婚，龜君再以「歲歲豐宴」與鼠輩立約，莊稼自此安寧。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: One year the Elephant had done a great deal of damage, breaking down the trees, drinking up the water in a time of scarcity, and eating the first tender crops from the fields. The King's hunters tried in vain to destroy him, for Elephant knew many charms and always escaped from their traps. At last the King offered the hand of his daughter in marriage to anyone who would rid the country of the pest. Tortoise went to the palace and offered to catch Elephant, and then made his preparations: outside the town a large pit was dug, and on the top of it was laid a thin platform covered with velvet cloths and leopard-skins, like a throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tortoise set off into the forest, accompanied by slaves and drummers, and told the astonished Elephant that the old King was dead and the people all wished Elephant to rule over them, because he was the greatest of all animals. Flattered, Elephant agreed to accompany him to the town — but when he went up onto the platform to be crowned King, the wood gave way beneath him, he crashed down into the pit, and was speedily slain by the King's hunters. All the people praised the cunning of Tortoise, who went to the palace to receive his bride; but the King refused to give his daughter to such an insignificant creature. In revenge, Tortoise called together all the field-mice and elves to eat up and carry away the new crops, and when famine threatened he was ready to help again — but only after the Princess became his bride. The King was forced to consent, and Tortoise then made the pests a feast and promised the same twice every year before the harvests if they agreed never to touch the corn in the fields. They consented, and after that the mice and elves never troubled the country again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXII (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba market town (symbolic pin: dancing-ground near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴市集（象徵定位：奧約近郊舞場）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIII

summary.en: Hungry Tortoise hides in the full sack his prosperous neighbour Mr. Fly carries to the dancing-ground each day and steals the thrown coins. Caught at last, the drummer beats the sack until Tortoise is black and blue — whence his bruised shell — and Mr. Fly drops him from the air before his own house; he and his wife Nyanribo flee the country in shame.
summary.zh: 龜家斷炊，鄰居蠅翁卻天天背袋赴舞場收錢。龜君藏入袋中連日偷錢，終被捉住。鼓師把袋口紮緊猛擂如鼓，打得龜背青一塊紫一塊——龜甲上的斑痕由此而來。蠅翁又高飛擲袋，正落在龜宅門前；妻子尼揚里博當眾開袋見夫，夫婦羞愧難當，遷往他鄉。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle, with shell-pattern etiology. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Once Tortoise and his family fell on hard times and had nothing to eat, but their neighbour Mr. Fly seemed very prosperous and feasted every night. Watching him, Tortoise discovered that Mr. Fly flew away every morning early with a large empty sack on his back and returned in the evening with the sack full. One morning Tortoise hid in the sack. Mr. Fly descended in the market-place of a large town, where drummers beat the tones of the dance and maidens danced before a crowd; when the people threw money, Mr. Fly picked the coins up and hid them in his sack. Tortoise quickly got out and took most of the money with him, so that poor Mr. Fly was surprised to find the sack almost empty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: This happened several times, until one day as he put money in the sack Mr. Fly caught sight of Tortoise hiding inside it. He told the drummer, who had been losing coins: "Look inside this sack and you will see the thief sitting among the money he has stolen." "How shall the thief be punished?" cried the drummer. "Just tie up the sack," said Mr. Fly, "and then beat upon it as if it were a drum." So the drummer tied up the sack and beat upon it until Tortoise was black and blue — and this is why his back is covered with bruises. Then Mr. Fly picked up the sack, flew high up in the air, and dropped it, by chance just outside Tortoise's house. When Nyanribo, his wife, opened the sack before a crowd, she found Tortoise inside, more dead than alive; Mr. Fly made a song narrating the whole story, and Tortoise and Nyanribo were so ashamed that they left the place and went to live in another country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Erin and Erinomi: Tortoise's Great Tug-of-War

region.en: Yoruba river-bank (symbolic pin: river-bank meeting place, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴河岸（象徵定位：奧約近郊河岸）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIV

summary.en: Mischievous Tortoise tells each of the two great elephants of land and water that the other calls him a weakling, and ropes them together for a strength test. Elephant hauls on land, Hippo hauls in the river, neither yields — until, meeting to drink, they discover the rope binds them to each other, and the trickster is long gone.
summary.zh: 陸象與河馬本是同源兄弟。好事的龜君分別告訴兩位：「對方譏你無力。」遂以粗繩將二者相繫，教他們較勁。象在岸上拖、馬在水中拽，誰也不肯認輸；直到相會喝水，才發現繩索兩端繫的正是彼此。二獸怒尋龜君，早已逃之夭夭。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise was always fond of making mischief between harmless people. One day as he walked along the river-bank he came upon the Elephant and said to him: "The Hippo is boasting that you are only a weakling, and that you have not strength to pull a log out of the river." "That is false!" cried the Elephant, and to prove his strength he allowed Tortoise to tie a strong rope to his trunk and attach the other end to a log in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tortoise went down to the water holding the rope and said to Hippo: "The Elephant is boasting of his strength, and he declares that you are a weakling and could not pull down a tree." "That is false!" cried the Hippo. "I can pull down any tree." Tortoise then said he had attached the rope to a tree, and fastened the other end to Hippo's horn. The two animals began to pull, one on each end of the rope; Elephant pulled and pulled, and the Hippo pulled and pulled, and neither gave way. After some time Hippo rested, and Elephant came down to the water to quench his thirst — and then they saw the trick that had been played on them. Snorting with anger, they began to look for the mischievous Tortoise, but by this time he was, you may be sure, very far away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIV (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba village (symbolic pin: village outskirts near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴村落（象徵定位：伊費近郊村外）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXV

summary.en: Tortoise's enemies try fire (he draws into his shell), drowning (the sun dries the pool), and burial (a treasure-digger unearths him at the bamboo stake). Three deaths escaped, he is left in peace — the charm is his shell.
summary.zh: 仇家三次謀害龜君：縱火燒屋——他縮入殼中安然無恙；拋入深池——烈日蒸乾池水；活埋土中——過路人誤以為竹樁下埋著寶藏，掘出的竟是熟睡的龜。三死不遂，仇家嘆服「他自有符咒」，自此不再相擾。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise had many enemies, and they plotted together to kill him. One night when Tortoise was asleep in his hut they set fire to it, and as they saw the flames leaping up they said: "He cannot escape. He will die." But Tortoise drew himself into his shell and was untouched by the fire, and in the morning his enemies were astonished to see him walking about as usual.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXV (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon they threw Tortoise into a pool of water: "The pool is deep. He will drown." But Tortoise had drawn himself into his shell and was secure, and at noon the sun shone fiercely and dried up the pool; that evening Tortoise walked about the village as if nothing had happened. The next day they buried him in a deep hole, marking the place with a bamboo stake. Meanwhile a passing man saw the stake and thought, "Someone has buried a treasure here!" He called his friends, and they began to dig — but all they found was Tortoise fast asleep inside his shell. He walked about the village again looking very happy, and his enemies were filled with astonishment: "He has a charm, and we shall never be able to kill him." And from that day they left him in peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXV (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba farmstead (symbolic pin: fowl-yard near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴農家（象徵定位：伊費近郊雞舍）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVI

summary.en: Starving, Tortoise frightens the fowls with a lie: the farmer's wife will kill the first to crow or cluck. All keep silent while Tortoise steals every egg; the cheated wife, finding the nests empty, slaughters the whole flock — and while the farmers feast on chicken, Tortoise and Nyanribo feast on eggs.
summary.zh: 飢腸轆轆的龜君向雞群謊報：「主婦明日要宰最先啼叫的那隻。」雞群噤若寒蟬，龜君趁夜遍偷雞蛋。主婦清晨見蛋巢盡空，盛怒之下把雞群殺個精光。農家大啖雞肉之時，龜君與尼揚里博正邀友大啖蛋宴。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: One day Tortoise and Nyanribo felt very hungry, but they could not afford to buy food. Tortoise heard a cock crowing, and it gave him an idea. He went to the cock and said: "I have come to warn you. I heard the farmer asking his wife to prepare chicken for dinner to-morrow." At this all the fowls were in great distress and wondered which of them was to be killed. Tortoise replied: "I heard the farmer's wife say that she will kill the first of you which she hears crowing or clucking in the morning." Naturally the fowls decided to be absolutely silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVI (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Very early in the morning Tortoise went creeping among the fowls and stole all the eggs from the nests, taking them one by one to his house; but the cock was afraid to crow and the hens were afraid to cluck, and when the farmer's wife came to collect the eggs she found that they had all been stolen. At this she flew into a rage and killed all the fowls instead of one, and while the farmer and his wife had a feast of chicken, Tortoise and Nyanribo invited their friends to a feast of eggs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVI (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise and Crab, the Two Boasters

region.en: Yoruba seashore (symbolic pin: lagoon shore near Lagos)
region.zh: 約魯巴海濱（象徵定位：拉哥斯近郊湖岸）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVII

summary.en: Tortoise and Crab fight to a draw on the seashore, neither shell able to hurt the other, and agree they are the strongest creatures in the world — until a boy picks up both: Tortoise is boiled, Crab goes into the stew. Their descendants are ashamed to meet ever since.
summary.zh: 龜與蟹在海邊決鬥，彼此硬甲相抗、互不能傷，於是自誇為「天下最強」。話音未落，一個少年把他倆一併拾走：龜被入鍋水煮、甲殼做飾物，蟹成了少年的晚餐。自此兩家子孫羞於相見，至今仍互相迴避。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; pride-punished folktale. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Everyone knows that Tortoise and Crab are enemies. One morning on the seashore they decided to fight to see which was the stronger, but, as both of them are protected by a hard shell, neither could succeed in injuring the other. Finally they came to an agreement that they were equal in strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: "We are so well protected by our armour," said Tortoise, "that no one can harm us." "And thus," said Crab, "we are the strongest creatures in the world." But at this moment a boy passed by and picked them both up. Tortoise was boiled in a pot and his shell was made into ornaments, while Crab was cooked in a stew for the boy's supper. Since that day the descendants of the two boasters have always been ashamed to meet, and that is why they always shun one another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVII (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Tortoise, Pigeon, and the Horses'-Head Tree

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: field with dead horse, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧約近郊荒田）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXVIII

summary.en: Tortoise feeds greedily at his cousins' feast and lets Pigeon wait hungry outside. On the river Pigeon drops him — onto a crocodile's back. Avenging himself, Pigeon plants a horse's head in a field; Tortoise tells the King that horses' heads grow there, stakes his life on it, and is condemned to fire when the head has vanished — until the birds beat out the flames and he is pardoned.
summary.zh: 龜君在表親家中獨享盛宴，讓背他渡河的鴿子在門外捱餓。歸途鴿子半河將他拋下，恰好落在鱷魚背上得以逃生。鴿子再施報復：把馬頭插在田裡如樹。龜君向國王誇口馬頭能如草木生長，國王以性命為注——馬頭已失，龜被判火刑。鴿子悔恨召集群鳥撲火救主，國王赦之，兩友和好離去。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise and Pigeon were often seen walking together, but Tortoise treated his friend badly and often played tricks on him. Once Tortoise invited Pigeon to visit his cousins; at the river Pigeon was forced to take Tortoise upon his back and fly across with him. At the cousins' house Tortoise left his friend standing at the door while a feast was eaten, and when the cousins asked him to invite his friend, the greedy Tortoise replied: "My friend is a silly fellow, he will not eat in a stranger's house, and he is so shy that he refuses to come in."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVIII (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the river-bank Pigeon took Tortoise up again, flew half-way across, and allowed him to fall — but by chance Tortoise landed on the back of a floating crocodile and descended safely at the bank. Pigeon flew ahead to a field where a dead horse lay, cut off its head, and stuck it in the ground as if it grew there like a plant. When Tortoise reached the field he went to the King and told him he knew a place where horses' heads grew like plants. "If this is true, I will reward you with a great treasure; but if it is false, you must die." The King and a crowd accompanied him to the field, but Pigeon had removed the head; Tortoise was condemned and thrown on a large fire. Then Pigeon repented of his trick, called together all the birds of the air; they came like a wind, beating out the fire with their wings, and so rescued Tortoise. The King pardoned him, and the two friends departed in safety.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXVIII (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba forest grove (symbolic pin: twin trees in the grove, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴樹叢（象徵定位：伊費近郊雙樹林）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XXXIX

summary.en: In famine-time Tortoise finds two trees: the little Chop-tree rains food at the words "Tree, do your duty!", while the great Whip-tree only beats. Feasting daily in secret, he grows fat as his family starves; Nyanribo follows him, feasts her whole household at the Chop-tree — and Tortoise's spite sends them under the Whip-tree, where they are beaten to death. When the King demands an accounting, Tortoise leads the court to the trees; the crowd beats itself, Tortoise hides in his shell, and forever after he hides at the words "Chop" and "Whip."
summary.zh: 饑荒之年，龜君在林中遇見兩棵樹：矮的「饗食樹」一經呼喚便落雨般的美食；高大的「鞭笞樹」卻只會抽打。他瞞著家人日日赴宴、日漸肥碩，妻兒卻面黃肌瘦。尼揚里博跟蹤發現後，率全家兒孫赴饗食樹下大快朵頤；龜君懷恨毒言，教他們站到鞭笞樹下——眾人竟被活活打死。國王逼其交代，他領群臣至樹下重演，國王親呼口訣而眾人遭殃。憤怒的群眾遍尋不得，龜君早已縮殼藏身；至今他一聽「饗食」「鞭笞」二字便躲入殼中。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: There was a famine in the land, and each day Tortoise went into the forest to find food, returning with only a few herbs and dried-up nut-kernels for his family. One day in a grove he saw two trees close together, a small stunted tree and a big tree with thick foliage. The little tree told him it was the Chop-tree, and at his words its branches waved and a shower of food fell to the ground, on which Tortoise ate until nothing remained. The splendid tall tree was named Whip-tree, and at Tortoise's question of what it could produce it bent its branches and beat him until he cried for mercy. Being greedy, Tortoise said nothing of the two trees, showed his wife only a few poor nuts, and went every day to the Chop-tree and feasted to his heart's content while his family and all the people, even to the King, grew thin — and Nyanribo began to suspect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIX (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nyanribo followed him, saw him say "Tree, do your duty!", and hastened back for the whole family of children and cousins, who feasted under the Chop-tree. But spiteful Tortoise was displeased and exclaimed: "I wish you would stand under the other tree and receive your proper reward!" They all went to stand under the Whip-tree, Nyanribo cried "Tree, do your duty!", and the branches began to beat them all soundly until they died. Tortoise hastily returned home, but the King soon ordered him to account for his family's disappearance. He led the King and all the nobles into the forest, feasted them under the Chop-tree, then asked them to stand underneath the other tree — and the King himself cried out "Tree, do your duty!" to terrible effect. In a great rage the people hunted for Tortoise, but he hid inside his shell in a secret place until the King died and a new King was found. Yet whenever he hears the two words Chop and Whip, he hides in his shell, thinking himself in danger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XXXIX (1929); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: open sky-road above Tortoise's compound, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊龜宅上空）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded by M. I. Ogumefu, published 1929

source.work: M. I. Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends (London: Sheldon Press, 1929), tale XL

summary.en: Tortoise contracts with a Cloud: "Pass!" for sunshine, "Fall!" for rain, payment in cowries laid on the ground. He sells fine weather to a wedding-chief and rain to a fisherman, keeps every cowrie, and grows rich — until the cheated Cloud, after once more granting his "Pass!", rolls back and drowns Tortoise and all his family in the flood he asked to be spared.
summary.zh: 龜君與雲訂約：喊「散！」便天晴，喊「落！」便下雨，每次以貝幣為酬。他先替愁雨的酋長婚宴求晴，又替漁夫求雨，貝幣全入私囊，愈發富貴。雲終於動怒：龜君出行喊「散！」，雲應聲退開——待他上路，雲又捲回，暴雨傾盆，洪水中龜君闔家淹斃。

sensitivity.note: Living Yoruba tradition; Tortoise (Ijapa) trickster cycle; ends in a local flood retribution, linking to the flood motif cluster. Archival record of a 1929 colonial-era collection.

passages.text: Tortoise and a Cloud once made the following agreement: whenever Tortoise very much desired fine weather, he was to stand outside his house and call "Pass! Pass!", and then the Cloud would roll away and allow the sun to shine; and when he desired rain, he was to cry "Fall! Fall!" and the rain would pour down. In payment Tortoise was to place a certain number of cowries on the ground each time. At first he duly paid, but on the occasion of a Chief's wedding he sold the Chief fine weather for a sum of cowries and kept the whole amount for himself. The next day he likewise sold rain to a man whose fishing-stakes needed a swollen river — "I will throw a spear into the clouds, and the rain will fall" — and again kept every cowrie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XL (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Soon, in this way, he grew rich and famous, almost every day someone asking for fine or rainy weather; he stored many bags of cowries in his house and gave nothing to the Cloud, pretending, when two customers clashed, that he had grown tired of holding up the clouds on his back. But seeing how rich Tortoise became, the hard-working Cloud was angry and decided to punish him. One day Tortoise wished to set out on a journey with his family, so he stood outside his house and cried: "Pass! Pass! Let the sun shine on my journey!" But as soon as he had set out, the Cloud rolled back again and rain poured down in torrents, causing a great flood in which Tortoise and all his family were drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ogumefu, Yoruba Legends, tale XL (1929); not verbatim.
